new_statements.quote: §. 16. Sanan pääpaino on yleensä sanan ensimäisellä tavulla; esim. àndoa, òttamas. Joskus harvoin pääpaino on toisella tai kolmannella tavulla; esim. ylèn, yhtèlleh, hurivòm, uràa. Paitsi pääpainoa on neli- ja useampitavuisilla sanoilla heikompi sivupaino kolmannella (tai neljännellä) ja viidennellä tavulla; esim. àndoàkseh, òttamàssah, kàččelèmmokseh, òpastumàtoi, òlemàttomùten. Liitännäispartikkelit i ja e ovat aina painollisia; esim. onì, soavè, voiè (vakuuttava vastaus kysymykseen: ongo, soavgo, voibigo); miè? kuiè? (kysymys mi? kui? uudistettuna).
new_statements.translation: § 16. The primary stress of a word is generally on the first syllable of the word; e.g. àndoa, òttamas. Occasionally, rarely, the primary stress is on the second or third syllable; e.g. ylèn, yhtèlleh, hurivòm, uràa. Besides the primary stress, words of four or more syllables have a weaker secondary stress on the third (or fourth) and fifth syllable; e.g. àndoàkseh, òttamàssah, kàččelèmmokseh, òpastumàtoi, òlemàttomùten. Unstressed are generally the second and the last syllable of the word (with the exceptions mentioned above and below). The enclitic particles i and e are always stressed; e.g. onì, soavè, voiè (affirmative answer to the question ongo, soavgo, voibigo); miè? kuiè? (the question mi? kui? repeated).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable; secondary stress on the third (or fourth) and fifth syllables of words of four or more syllables, i.e. alternating odd syllables; second and final syllables unstressed. Corroborated for the whole of Karelian incl. six Livvi grammars by Novak et al. 2022: 81 ('The primary stress always falls on the first syllable.. secondary stress.. on every odd syllable.. excluding the last one').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Weaker secondary stress on the 3rd (or 4th) and 5th syllables of words with four or more syllables (Ahtia § 16); Novak et al. 2022: 81 add that in compounds the secondary stress falls on the first syllable of the second component and that primary and secondary stress never fall on consecutive syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Rarely, primary stress on the 2nd or 3rd syllable in a handful of (emphatic/particle-like) words: ylèn, yhtèlleh, hurivòm, uràa; the enclitic particles i and e are always stressed (onì, soavè, voiè, miè?, kuiè?). Novak et al. 2022: 81 add late Russian loans that may keep non-initial stress in dialects (but not in the standard varieties).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sanan pääpaino), descriptive grammar of the spoken Aunus (Livvi) dialects of Riipuskala (Salmi) and Säämäjärvi plus transitional Suojärvi, intended as a common literary norm; the same generalisation is reported by Novak et al. 2022 for every Karelian grammar they survey, including Genetz 1884: 125, Markianova 2002: 19 and Pyöli 2011: 20 for Livvi.
new_statements.identity_note: Ahtia 1938 describes the Aunus (Olonets = Livvi, livv1243) dialects of Riipuskala in Salmi and of Säämäjärvi, plus Suojärvi, which the preface itself calls a transitional dialect between Aunus and Viena (Novak et al. 2022 classify the book as a normative grammar of a proposed common literary Karelian built on Livvi Rypushkalitsy/Syamozero and Karelian Proper Suojärvi). The stress rule is stated for the language as a whole, and Novak et al. 2022: 81 report the same rule from all six Livvi grammars they analysed (incl. Genetz 1884: 125, Markianova 2002: 19, Pyöli 2011: 20), so it holds for Livvi proper, not only the Border-Karelian varieties. Genetz 1877 (also saved) describes Karelian Proper (krl), not Livvi.

new_statements.quote: Word stress in Karelian is constant. The primary stress always falls on the first syllable (pái-men / pái-moi ’a shepherd’), with the exception of some late Russian borrowings, in which the primary stress may sometimes fall on other syllables. In the standard varieties of Karelian stress can only be on the first syllable. The Karelian language always features secondary stress, which usually falls on every odd syllable of a compound noun, excluding the last one, while the second and even syllables remain unstressed (méč-čä-níek-ka / méč-čy-níek-ku ’a hunter’). A primary and secondary stress cannot, therefore, fall on consecutive syllables.
new_statements.citation: Novak, I. P; Penttonen, M; Ruuskanen, A; Siilin, L. 2019. Karel'skij jazyk v grammatikah: sravnitel'noe issledovanie fonetičeskoj i morfologičeskoj sistem. Petrozavodsk: KarRC RAS.

Surrounding section read: dynamic stress, no reduction; secondary stress on odd syllables, final syllable usually unstressed, Ludic apocope exception (mec-nik), compounds (py-ha|pai-vy), stress may be lost/move in the speech stream; Russian loans get stress moved to the first syllable with a long vowel/diphthong repla…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (fixed initial) and as the Ahtia 1938 § 16 statement, which it cites (Ahtia 1938: 10) along with Genetz 1884: 125, Markianova 2002: 19 and Pyöli 2011: 20 for Livvi; adds the secondary-stress rule (odd syllables, compounds), the Russian-loan exception and the loan-adaptation mechanism. The open copy at the listed KRC directory is the 2022 English translation, not the 2019 Russian book itself; the Russian original is not among the 104 the Internet Archive-captured files of that directory and the KRC hosts could not be reached by automated download.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic, constant word stress: primary stress on the first syllable of every content word, in all Karelian varieties including Livvi; only some late Russian loans may keep non-initial stress in dialects, and in the standard varieties stress is initial without exception.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every odd (3rd, 5th..) syllable except the last, i.e. alternating trochaic rhythm; final syllable normally unstressed; in compounds primary stress on the first syllable of the first member and secondary on the first syllable of the second member (pý-hä|pä́i-vy 'Sunday'); in apocope dialects (Ludic) a final syllable can carry secondary stress; stress may be lost or shift in connected speech.
new_statements.exceptions: Some late Russian borrowings may have primary stress on a non-initial syllable in dialects; otherwise Russian loans move stress to the first syllable, with the Russian stressed vowel replaced by a long vowel or diphthong (sámovuaru < samovár).
new_statements.identity_note: Novak et al. describe the Karelian language as a whole (Karelian Proper, Livvi-Karelian and Ludic, plus the standard varieties), built from 21 grammars of which six are Livvi (incl. Genetz 1884, Ahtia 1938, Markianova 2002, Pyöli 2011); slash-separated forms are dialect variants and the Livvi forms are pái-moi, méč-čy-níek-ku, pý-hä|pä́i-vy, sámovuaru. The word-stress statement therefore covers Livvi explicitly but is not Livvi-specific; the apocope remark (méč-ník) concerns Ludic.

Paino § 16, p. 10 (PDF p. 19): primary stress normally on the first syllable; rarely on 2nd/3rd (ylèn, yhtèlleh, hurivòm, uràa); weaker secondary stress on the 3rd (or 4th) and 5th syllables of words of 4+ syllables; 2nd and final syllables unstressed; enclitic particles i and e always stressed. Preface: material from Suojärvi, Riipuskala (Salmi) and Säämäjärvi, 'kuuluvat aunuksen murteen alaan' (= Livvi), Suojärvi being transitional between Aunus and Viena.
